claims.text: The starting material is a single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy with a uniform disordered solid solution and no detectable precipitates or grain-boundary segregation.
Service-relevant thermal exposure can trigger phase decomposition in a high-entropy alloy.
Cyclic mechanical loading at elevated temperature can trigger incipient solute segregation.
Thermal exposure causes incipient solute segregation in the initially homogeneous alloy.
Local solute segregation nucleates nanoscale ordered precipitates preferentially at grain boundaries or other internal interfaces.
The ordered precipitates may be B2 or similar intermetallic phases.
The proposed ordered precipitates are brittle.
Thermal activation promotes local atomic rearrangement and compositional fluctuations in the high-entropy matrix.
Applied stress promotes local atomic rearrangement and compositional fluctuations in the high-entropy matrix.
Ordered phases at internal interfaces create localized stress concentrators.
Interfacial ordered phases facilitate intergranular crack propagation.
Interfacial precipitation and the resulting crack propagation reduce toughness and promote brittle crack initiation.
Aged or elevated-temperature cyclically loaded samples will have lower impact energy or fracture toughness than the as-cast control.
The predicted toughness decrease will coincide with detectable nanoscale ordered precipitates at internal interfaces.
The proposed behavior is expected under moderate-to-high temperatures and sustained or cyclic mechanical loading.
At very low temperatures or under very rapid loading, phase decomposition may not have enough time to develop.
The phase stability and decomposition length scale depend on alloy composition and annealing temperature.
The type, size, distribution, and kinetics of precipitates may vary with alloy composition and loading history.
Concurrent deformation mechanisms may mask or interact with the proposed embrittlement process.
